::: notes
Welcome to the third day. Yesterday you reproduced a recorded result, worked the menu and declared one analysis, and two of the decisions in your declaration were about the estimator and the inference. Today we go underneath those decisions, and this first session is about the country-year panel itself. We start from the plainest model, one line through 270 points, and ask why its standard errors are wrong. Then fixed effects, in the two designs that divide the curve of the claim, and what each of them absorbs. Then the standard errors again, because 27 countries of very unequal weight carry all the evidence. We end with random effects and the within–between model, which shows that the comparison within countries and the comparison between them point in opposite directions. Twice along the way you fit the models yourselves.
:::

# PART 1 – The panel and the linear model {#part-1-the-panel-and-the-linear-model .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 1
:::

::: notes
Part one starts at the level at which the course works, the country-year, and with the simplest model that can be fitted there. A straight line through 270 points looks like a reasonable first try, and the reasons for its failure tell us what every later model of this session is for. Its standard errors pretend that the 270 rows are independent, and its slope mixes two comparisons that the claim keeps apart. Clustered standard errors repair the first problem and leave the second as it was.
:::

## The country-year panel {#the-country-year-panel .smaller}

::: {.small}
- The original author (OA) modelled the respondents of sixteen Eurobarometer waves directly [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic]. The course averages the 416,698 respondents into **270 country-years**, 27 member states in each of 10 years, 2004–2013
- The predictor varies only at that level. Every respondent interviewed in Germany in 2010 shares one German unemployment rate, so the information about the slope comes from 270 pairings of a rate and a mean, however many people were interviewed
- Each wave draws a new sample, so the respondents are repeated cross-sections, while the countries form a balanced panel: "insofar as societies are units of analysis ... in an important sense the data derived from such surveys are in fact panel data, since societies are each observed multiple times" [@Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling, p. 122]
- An association among the means of country-years need not hold among people [@Robinson1950EcologicalCorrelationsBehavior], and the next session takes up the respondents
:::

::: notes
The panel that the course ships has 270 rows, and behind them stand more than four hundred thousand people interviewed in sixteen Eurobarometer waves. The original author, the OA, modelled those people directly, whereas the course averages them into one row for each country and year. For this claim the averaging loses almost nothing, because the predictor is a national figure: everyone interviewed in Germany in 2010 shares one unemployment rate. So the evidence about the slope comes from 270 pairings, however many people stand behind each pairing. Fairbrother makes a point about vocabulary here. The people are new in every wave, but the countries are observed again and again, and in that sense the data are a panel. What the averages cannot tell us is how individuals respond, and that is the subject of the next session.
:::

## Pooled OLS {#pooled-ols .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](eu-frames-panel-data_files/figure-revealjs/d3-pooled-scatter-1.png){width=480}
:::
:::

:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.small}
- One line for every country and every year: $\bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ct}$
- `lm()`, `fixest::feols(vcov = "iid")` and `plm::plm(model = "pooling")` return the same numbers, because they fit one estimator under three names
- Slope −0.00110, t = −1.04, R^2^ = 0.4%: no association worth reporting
- On the same rows, the value recorded for C6HJR is t = −3.804, so the difference lies in the structure of the model
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
companion/panel-data.qmd, sections 2 and 3; cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy.csv.
:::

::: notes
Here is the plainest model, one line through all 270 country-years. On a panel it is called pooled OLS, because it pools every country and every year into one cloud. Three functions in R fit it, lm, fixest and plm, and they agree to the last digit once fixest is asked for classical standard errors. That is a habit worth keeping: make different functions agree on a model that you understand before you change anything. Now read the result. The slope is close to zero, its t is about minus one, and the line explains almost none of the variation. Yet the value recorded for C6HJR, on exactly these rows, is a t of minus three point eight. The data are the same in both fits, so the difference comes from the structure of the model, and the rest of the session takes that structure apart.
:::

## Clustered standard errors {#clustered-standard-errors .smaller}

::: {.small}
- The ten Danish rows share everything durable about Denmark. Those shared features sit in $\varepsilon$, so the errors of one country are correlated, while classical standard errors treat the 270 rows as 270 independent pieces of evidence
- **Cluster-robust standard errors** allow any pattern of correlation within a country. Only the standard error changes, never $\hat\beta$, and in such data "default standard errors can greatly overstate estimator precision" [@CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust, p. 317]
:::

```{.r}
fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes, cluster = ~cntry)
```

::: {.fragment .small}
Clustering by country multiplies the standard error of the pooled slope by 2.1, and its t falls from −1.04 to −0.50.
:::

::: {.src}
companion/panel-data.qmd, section 3.
:::

::: notes
The standard errors of that model assume that the 270 errors are independent, and they are not. The ten Danish rows share everything durable about Denmark, its institutions, its language, its standing view of Europe, and whatever the model leaves out about a country sits in the error, so the errors of one country move together. The first repair keeps the estimate and corrects its uncertainty. Cluster-robust standard errors let the errors inside each country be correlated in any pattern, and in fixest they take one argument. Cameron and Miller, whose guide is the standard reference, warn that default standard errors can greatly overstate precision in data of this kind. [advance] Here the standard error doubles and the t halves, because the 270 rows were never 270 independent pieces of evidence.
:::

## The pooled slope {#the-pooled-slope .smaller}

::: {.small}
- A pooled slope blends two comparisons: how framing moves when unemployment rises within a country, and how framing differs between countries with high and with low unemployment
- The cross-section carries much of the weight: 46.5% of the variance of unemployment and 65.1% of the variance of the cosmopolitan share lie between the 27 country means
- Swapped into each of the 864 specifications of the curve, pooled OLS puts 52.1% of its fits below zero, against 98.1% of the curve, and a fit and its twin on the curve fall on opposite sides of zero in 49.8% of the pairs
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The sign belongs to the estimate, so clustering cannot change it. Pooled OLS stays off the curve as an option of the Estimator decision, and Part 4 estimates the two comparisons one at a time.
:::

::: {.src}
companion/panel-data.qmd, section 3; cases/eu-frames/data/menu_deviations.csv.
:::

::: notes
Clustering repairs the uncertainty, and that leaves the estimate itself as the problem. A pooled model absorbs no differences between countries, so its slope mixes two comparisons: what happens to framing when unemployment rises within a country, and how countries with high unemployment differ from countries with low unemployment. Nearly half of the variance of unemployment lies between the country means, and about two thirds of the variance of the outcome, so the cross-section weighs heavily in the blend. Nor is the blend a quirk of one specification. Swap pooled OLS into every specification of the curve, and about half of the fits land below zero, where nearly all of the curve lies, and in half of the pairs, the two fits fall on opposite sides of zero. [advance] That is why pooled OLS stays off the curve, and why part four estimates the two comparisons one at a time.
:::

# PART 2 – Fixed effects {#part-2-fixed-effects .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 2
:::

::: notes
Part two goes after the estimate itself. Fixed effects give every country an intercept of its own, and in the two-way design every year as well, so that the slope comes only from how a country changes against itself. We look at what the effects absorb and at what they cannot reach, and then at the two designs that the menu offered you yesterday under the Estimator decision, which divide the curve of the claim more than any other decision does. The part ends with your first run of the session.
:::

## Two-way fixed effects {#two-way-fixed-effects .smaller}

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta\, x_{ct} + \alpha_c + \gamma_t + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

::: {.small}
- $\alpha_c$, an intercept for each country, absorbs everything constant about a country over the decade: its language, its institutions, its size, its standing enthusiasm for the EU
- $\gamma_t$, an intercept for each year, absorbs everything common to the 27 countries in that year, including the shared path of the crisis
- 26 country dummies and 9 year dummies in `lm()`, or the within transformation, which subtracts the country and the year means, give the same $\hat\beta$; `fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp | cntry + year)` takes the second route
- Slope −0.00347, t = −3.804 on 233 df, the value recorded for C6HJR. The within R^2^ of 0.058 is the share of the variation within countries that the slope explains
:::

::: {.src}
companion/panel-data.qmd, section 4.
:::

::: notes
This is the model that C6HJR fitted and that some of you reproduced yesterday: an intercept for each country and one for each year. The country intercepts take up everything that stays the same about a country across the decade, whether anyone measured it or not, so the slope never compares Denmark with Greece. The year intercepts take up whatever moved all of Europe together in a given year. What remains is each country compared with itself, net of the common movement of that year. Two routes give the same number: thirty-five dummies in lm, or the within transformation, which subtracts the country and year means from both sides and which fixest uses. The slope is minus point zero zero three five, with a t of minus three point eight. Of the two R-squared lines that fixest prints, only the within one bears on the question, and it is about six per cent.
:::

## What the fixed effects absorb {#what-the-fixed-effects-absorb .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.small}
**Absorbed**

- Any variable that is constant within a country, or within a year, measured or not
- The part of unemployment that is common to all countries in a year: 29.2% of its variation within countries, and 58.6% of the variation of GDP growth, above all the recession of 2009
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.small}
**Not absorbed**

- A confounder that changes within a country over the decade: a scandal, a programme of austerity, a swing in the stance of the governing party on Europe
- Feedback from framing to the economy [@LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse]
- No predictor is absorbed by a random intercept, and clustering changes only the standard errors
:::
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .small}
"there is widespread, though not well articulated, opinion that in panel analysis the usual obstacles to inference and estimation are suspended for the benefit of the analyst", the warning of Otis Dudley Duncan with which @Halaby2004PanelModelsSociological [p. 507] opens a review of panel models in sociology.
:::

::: notes
A fixed effect absorbs every variable that is constant within its group, measured or not, and that is its great strength. The national unemployment rate is constant neither within a country nor within a year, so both sets of effects leave it in the model and use only the part of it that is specific to a country-year. The year effects take away more than you might expect: almost a third of the movement of unemployment within countries, and well over half of the movement of growth, much of it the recession of 2009, which reached every member state at once. On the right, what fixed effects cannot reach: anything that changes within a country over the decade and moves both unemployment and framing, and feedback from framing to the economy. [advance] The warning of Duncan is still worth reading aloud: panel data do not suspend the usual obstacles to inference.
:::

## The two designs {#the-two-designs .smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](eu-frames-panel-data_files/figure-revealjs/d3-curve-by-design-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
- With country effects alone, the design of KQXUE, the slope is −0.00564 against −0.00347, because the comparison keeps the change that every member state went through in the same year
- Two questions: did framing fall in the years in which unemployment rose by more than the European movement of that year, or in the years in which unemployment was high, whatever happened elsewhere?
- The Estimator decision carries 41.5% of the variance of the claim-aligned r across the curve, more than any other decision. Below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 are 92.6% of the specifications with country effects alone and 61.8% of the two-way ones
:::

::: notes
The design that KQXUE fitted has an intercept for each country and none for the year, and on the course panel its slope is larger by more than half. Without year effects, the comparison of a country with itself keeps the change that every member state went through in the same year. So the two slopes answer two questions. The two-way design asks whether framing fell in the years in which a country's unemployment rose by more than the European movement of that year. The country design asks whether it fell in the years in which unemployment was high, whatever happened elsewhere, which leaves it open to any shift in framing across Europe that coincided with the crisis. Both are defensible readings of the claim, and the curve keeps both. The chart shows what the choice does: the orange specifications, with country effects alone, sit further below zero, and this one decision carries more of the variance of the curve than any other.
:::

## Hands-on 1 – The two designs {#hands-on-1-the-two-designs .smaller}

::: {.small}
**In the workspace**, in the console or in a chunk of your own:

1. Read the panel, fit the pooled model and the two designs, and set them side by side:

   ```{.r}
   euframes <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
   pooled  <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp, data = euframes, cluster = ~cntry)
   two_way <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp | cntry + year, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")
   country <- fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp | cntry, data = euframes, vcov = "iid")
   fixest::etable(pooled, two_way, country)
   ```
2. Add the mean unemployment of each country to the two-way model, and read what fixest does with it:

   ```{.r}
   euframes_wb <- datawizard::demean(euframes, select = "unemp", by = "cntry")
   fixest::feols(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_between | cntry + year, data = euframes_wb, vcov = "iid")
   ```
3. **Which design does your declaration of Task 5 use, and which of the two questions does it ask?** One sentence for your notes
:::

::: notes
Your turn, in the workspace. Read the panel in the console, fit the pooled model with errors clustered by country and the two designs with classical errors, and set the three side by side with etable. The pooled slope sits near zero, and the two designs give the slopes of the last slide. Then a test of absorption. The demean function of datawizard returns the mean unemployment of each country over the decade, and when you add that mean to the two-way model, fixest removes it for collinearity, because the country effects already hold it, and the slope of unemployment does not move by a digit. Last, look back at your preregistration block: which design did you declare, and which question does it ask? Write the sentence down, because the report of this afternoon needs it. [state the time]
:::

# PART 3 – Few clusters {#part-3-few-clusters .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 3
:::

::: notes
Part three returns to the standard errors, now of the two-way design. Yesterday you met the CR2 test as the rule that classes every point of the curve. Today we look at why the course needs it. The years of one country resemble each other, and once the fixed effects have done their work, a handful of countries hold most of the variation that identifies the slope. With few clusters of such unequal weight, even the usual clustered test overstates the evidence.
:::

## Errors that persist {#errors-that-persist .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](eu-frames-panel-data_files/figure-revealjs/d3-residual-persistence-1.png){width=480}
:::
:::

:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.small}
- The residual of a country in one year correlates with its residual in the year before at **0.53**
- A country that framed the EU more positively than the model expects in one year tends to do so in the next, so ten years of one country carry less information than ten independent observations
- Clustering by country allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and with G = 27 countries the clustered t is referred to G − 1 = 26 degrees of freedom
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
companion/panel-data.qmd, section 4.
:::

::: notes
Here are the residuals of the two-way model, each country-year against the same country in the year before, and they line up. The correlation is about a half, so a country that framed the EU more positively than the model expects in one year tends to do so in the next year as well. Ten years of one country therefore carry less information than ten independent observations would, and the classical standard errors, which treat them as independent, are too small. Clustering by country is the repair that you met in part one. It allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and with twenty-seven countries the clustered t is referred to twenty-six degrees of freedom. That gives the second row of the table that you met yesterday, and it is not yet the rule of the curve.
:::

## Countries of unequal weight {#countries-of-unequal-weight .smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](eu-frames-panel-data_files/figure-revealjs/d3-variation-share-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
- Once the country and year effects are removed, the variation in unemployment that identifies the slope sits mostly in a few countries: Greece holds 17.5%, Spain 15.9% and Poland 10.6%
- With few clusters of such unequal weight, even the clustered test overstates the evidence. Few clusters are "the most difficult complication to deal with", and "[t]here is no clear-cut definition of 'few'; depending on the situation, 'few' may range from less than 20 to less than 50 clusters in the balanced case" [@CameronMiller2015PractitionersGuideClusterrobust, p. 319]
:::

::: notes
Clustering assumes that the countries bring similar amounts of information, and here they do not. Once the country and year effects have taken their share, the variation in unemployment that is left, which is all that identifies the slope, sits mostly in a few countries. Greece holds about a sixth of it, Spain nearly as much and Poland about a tenth, while the smallest countries hold almost nothing. A slope estimated mostly from three countries has, in effect, few clusters behind it, whatever the count says. Cameron and Miller call few clusters the most difficult complication of the whole subject, and they decline to say how few is few: anything from fewer than twenty to fewer than fifty, depending on the design. Twenty-seven countries of this unequal weight sit well inside that range.
:::

## The CR2 test {#the-cr2-test .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **CR2** [@BellMcCaffrey2002BiasReductionStandard] enlarges the residuals of each country by the amount by which that country pulled the fit towards itself, since the residuals of a country that carries much of the variation come out too small
- Its t is referred to **Satterthwaite degrees of freedom** [@PustejovskyTipton2018SmallsampleMethodsClusterrobust], which say how many clusters effectively carry the information: close to G − 1 when the clusters weigh alike, far fewer when a few of them dominate
- The combination keeps the share of false rejections close to the 5% that the test promises [@ImbensKolesar2016RobustStandardErrors]. The wild cluster bootstrap is the resampling answer [@MacKinnonWebb2017WildBootstrapInference], and the course leaves it aside because its only implementation in R is no longer maintained
:::

```{.r}
m_lsdv <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + factor(cntry) + factor(year), data = euframes)
clubSandwich::coef_test(m_lsdv, vcov = "CR2", cluster = euframes$cntry, coefs = "unemp",
                        test = "Satterthwaite")
```

::: {.src}
companion/panel-data.qmd, section 4. The test needs the dummy-variable fit, because the correction works on the full design matrix.
:::

::: notes
The remedy that the course uses is the CR2 correction of Bell and McCaffrey. The ordinary clustered formula takes the residuals of each country as they come out of the fit. But when one country carries much of the variation, the fit has already been pulled towards that country, so its residuals are too small, and the standard error with them. CR2 enlarges the residuals of each country by the amount by which that country pulled the fit. Its test then uses Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which say how many countries effectively carry the information. Imbens and Kolesár recommend this combination for few and unequal clusters, because it keeps the false rejections near the promised five per cent. It takes one call to clubSandwich, on the dummy-variable fit, and it returns the p-value stored on the curve exactly, since nothing in it is random.
:::

# PART 4 – Within and between {#part-4-within-and-between .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 4
:::

::: notes
The last part sits between the two extremes of this session, pooled OLS, which ignores the countries, and fixed effects, which give each country an intercept of its own. Random effects keep a term for each country but treat it as a draw from a distribution, and the assumption that econometrics attaches to them fails on this panel. The within–between model shows why: it estimates the comparison within countries and the comparison between them side by side, and the two point in opposite directions. This is also where the session hands over to the next one, on multilevel models.
:::

## Random effects {#random-effects .smaller}

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{ct} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct}, \qquad u_c \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) $$

::: {.small}
- One variance in place of 27 intercepts. Generalised least squares subtracts a fraction θ of each country mean, so that θ = 0 gives pooled OLS and θ = 1 fixed effects. On the panel θ = 0.78, and the slope, −0.00525, lies near the −0.00564 of country fixed effects
- The assumption: "In modern econometric parlance, a random effects framework is synonymous with zero correlation between the observed explanatory variables and the unobserved effect" [@Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross, p. 286]
- The Hausman test of the two one-way designs rejects it, p = 0.0017 [@Hausman1978SpecificationTestsEconometrics], although its traditional form assumes errors that are uncorrelated from year to year, which a residual correlation of 0.53 rules out
:::

::: {.src}
companion/panel-data.qmd, section 5.
:::

::: notes
Random effects keep a term for each country, but in place of twenty-seven intercepts they estimate one number, the variance of the country effects. The estimator subtracts a fraction of each country mean, theta, so it sits on a line that runs from pooled OLS, at nought, to fixed effects, at one. Here theta is about point eight, and the slope duly lands near the answer of country fixed effects. The price is an assumption, which in econometrics has become the meaning of the term: the country effects must be unrelated to the predictor. On this panel that is hard to believe, because the level of unemployment of a country is bound up with the same durable features that shape its view of Europe. The Hausman test agrees, but its classical form assumes away the persistence that part three found, so the next slide gives the comparison a form that our CR2 rule can test.
:::

## The within–between model {#the-within-between-model .smaller}

$$ \bar{y}_{ct} = \beta_0 + \beta_W (x_{ct} - \bar{x}_{c\cdot}) + \beta_B\, \bar{x}_{c\cdot} + u_c + \varepsilon_{ct} $$

::: {.small}
- Unemployment is split into the mean of each country over the decade and the departure of each year from that mean, each with a slope of its own [@Mundlak1978PoolingTimeSeries; @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects]
- Within, **−0.00564**, the slope with country fixed effects to the last digit. Between, **+0.00414**, positive and imprecise (p = 0.31 on 25 df). The pooled slope of −0.00110 blended the two
- The difference between the two slopes holds under CR2, p = 0.040 on 9.3 df, and under the errors of the model, p = 0.024. The Hausman test, "[a]lthough often (mis)used as a test of whether FE or RE models 'should' be used ..., it is really a test of whether there is a contextual effect, or whether the between and within effects are different" [@BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects, p. 1057]
:::

::: notes
Bell and Jones propose a more informative answer than picking a winner between fixed and random effects. Split unemployment into the average of each country over the decade and the departure of each year from that average, and give each part a slope of its own. The within slope is exactly the slope with country fixed effects, because separating out the variation between countries is what fixed effects do. The between slope is positive and imprecise. And the pooled slope of part one turns out to be a weighted blend of the two, two patterns of opposite sign averaged into something near zero. The difference between the slopes holds under our CR2 rule as well as under the errors of the model, so for this outcome the assumption of random effects fails under every test that the course applies, and Bell and colleagues read the Hausman test in exactly these terms, as a test of whether the two slopes differ.
:::

::: {.small}
- Across the 27 countries the association is positive, with a correlation of 0.20 between the two sets of means; within countries it is negative, with a CR2 p of 0.0072
- 'The effect of unemployment on EU framing' has a value within countries and a value between them, and choosing a model means choosing which of the two you ask about. The claim, as the curve reads it, is about change within countries, and the cross-national question has its answer in the regression on country means, outside the curve
:::

::: notes
Here are the two associations. On the left each country is one point, its average unemployment over the decade against its average cosmopolitan share, and the line across them rises: the countries with more unemployment did not frame the EU in less cosmopolitan terms, if anything the reverse. On the right each country-year is a departure from the averages of its own country, and within countries the line falls. The two associations answer different questions. 'The effect of unemployment on EU framing' has a value within countries and a value between them, and choosing a model means choosing which of the two you ask about. The claim, as the curve reads it, is about change within countries. Anyone who wants the cross-national answer has it on the left, in the regression on the country means, and it lies outside the curve.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – Within and between {#hands-on-2-within-and-between .smaller}

::: {.small}
**In the workspace**, with `euframes` and `euframes_wb` from Hands-on 1:

1. The CR2 test of the two-way slope, which should return the t, the df and the p of the table:

   ```{.r}
   m_lsdv <- lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + factor(cntry) + factor(year), data = euframes)
   clubSandwich::coef_test(m_lsdv, vcov = "CR2", cluster = euframes$cntry, coefs = "unemp",
                           test = "Satterthwaite")
   ```
2. The within–between model, whose within slope should equal the slope of `country` in Hands-on 1:

   ```{.r}
   m_wb <- lmerTest::lmer(mcosmo ~ unemp_within + unemp_between + (1 | cntry), data = euframes_wb)
   parameters::model_parameters(m_wb, effects = "fixed", ci_method = "satterthwaite")
   ```
3. Fit `lm(mcosmo ~ unemp + unemp_between + factor(year), data = euframes_wb)` and check that the coefficient on `unemp` is now the two-way slope. **What does the coefficient on `unemp_between` compare in this design?**
:::

::: notes
Your last run of the session. First the CR2 test, one call to clubSandwich on the dummy-variable fit, which should give you the t, the degrees of freedom and the p of the table to the last digit. Then the within–between model with lmer, using the two columns that demean made for you in the first hands-on, and check that the within slope equals the slope of the country design that you fitted then. Last, the step that joins the two halves of the session: add a dummy for each year to the pooled Mundlak regression. The year dummies remove the common European path, as the year effects did, so the coefficient on unemployment becomes the two-way slope. Then say in one sentence what the coefficient on the country mean compares in that design. [state the time]
:::
